analysis.one_liner: Gives buyers a tax credit worth up to $2 million for purchasing a new U.S.-built luxury yacht.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and never received a House vote, dying in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a tax credit covering 20% of the cost of a new yacht, up to $2 million, for buyers of yachts over 50 feet built in the United States. It also would have created a $25 million Commerce Department grant program to market U.S.-built yachts to foreign buyers and to train shipyard workers. The credit would be recaptured — partly repaid — if the yacht were sold or moved overseas in its first seven years.
analysis.who_benefits: Buyers of new U.S.-built yachts over 50 feet long would get a tax credit worth up to $2 million, a subsidy only available to people who can already afford a multi-million-dollar vessel. U.S. yacht builders would gain a large new incentive pulling customers toward domestically built boats, and shipyard workers would gain from any resulting demand and from the authorized worker-training grants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy yacht buyers and U.S. yacht builders

how_it_helps.text: Buyers would receive a credit of 20% of the cost of a new U.S.-built yacht over 50 feet, capped at $2 million per yacht, with unused credit carried forward to later years [S3].

The credit would be repaid on a sliding scale (100% in year one, phasing to zero after seven years) if the yacht were sold or documented, registered, maintained, or stored outside the U.S., keeping the subsidy tied to domestic ownership and use [S3].

The bill would authorize $25 million in Commerce Department grants to encourage foreign buyers to purchase U.S.-built luxury yachts and to provide specialized training for yacht-construction workers [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would bear the cost through reduced income tax revenue from the credit and through appropriations for the grant program. Because only buyers of yachts over 50 feet qualify, the benefit would flow to a small group of wealthy purchasers, and the public would subsidize each purchase with no direct return.

drawbacks.text: The credit is a direct transfer to buyers of multi-million-dollar yachts, a benefit unavailable to ordinary households, and the maximum $2 million credit would cost the Treasury up to that amount per yacht purchased [S3].
The grant program would spend up to $25 million in public funds partly on marketing luxury yachts to foreign buyers, a use of tax dollars with no broad public benefit [S3].

A supporter would argue the bill supports U.S. shipyard jobs and keeps luxury yacht construction from moving overseas, and the recapture rules and Buy-American requirements show an effort to tie the subsidy to domestic work [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Any job gains at U.S. yacht yards would come at the price of a large tax subsidy targeted exclusively at wealthy yacht purchasers plus a $25 million grant program, much of it aimed at marketing luxury goods abroad. For most households the costs would show up as federal revenue foregone, while the benefits would be concentrated on a small wealthy group and one regional industry. Weighed plainly, the public costs outweighed any broad public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to two House committees, and referred to a subcommittee, and then nothing further happened before that Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsor ever signed on.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick J. Kennedy (D-RI) introduced the bill on February 10, 1999 [S5].
It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee (which handles tax credits) and to the Commerce Committee, splitting jurisdiction between the two [S5].
On March 1, 1999, the Commerce Committee's portion was referred to its Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection [S5].
No further action was taken for the rest of the 106th Congress, which ended January 3, 2001 [S1] [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors during its two years in the House [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers are better off because the bill died — no multi-million-dollar-per-yacht tax credit and no $25 million luxury-boat marketing program were enacted. The bill's intended beneficiaries, wealthy yacht buyers and U.S. yacht builders, did not receive the subsidy.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers; the subsidy never became law

for.name: Rep. Patrick J. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it never attracted a cosponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of primary jurisdiction over the tax-credit provision
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral on February 10, 1999 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Commerce Committee and its Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection
against.role: Second committee of referral (grant program provisions)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittee on March 1, 1999 and took no further action; the bill died without a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan alignment can be measured from the record.

industries.industry: U.S. luxury yacht builders and shipyards
industries.note: The bill would have handed the industry a 20% purchase credit worth up to $2 million per yacht plus $25 million in federal marketing and worker-training grants — a large public subsidy for building luxury goods. It died, so the industry gained nothing.

Buyers of new U.S.-built yachts over 50 feet — by definition people who can spend millions on a vessel — would have received up to $2 million per yacht in tax relief paid for by all taxpayers. The bill died, so no subsidy was paid.

The credit required yachts to be designed, built, documented, and registered in the U.S. and recaptured if moved abroad, so it would have pulled buyers away from foreign-built yachts. Foreign builders benefited instead when the bill died.
